title: Span<T>, Memory<T> and ref structs
body: `Span<T>` is a view over a contiguous region of memory: part of an array, a `stackalloc` buffer or native memory. Slicing a span (`span[2..5]` or `Slice`) creates another view without copying. `ReadOnlySpan<T>` is the read-only version; `string.AsSpan()` gives a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` so you can parse substrings without allocating new strings.

Span is a `ref struct`: it may live only on the stack. It cannot be a field of a class, be boxed, be captured by a lambda or (until C# 13's relaxations) live across an `await` or `yield`. These rules let the compiler guarantee a span never outlives the memory it points to. `stackalloc int[16]` assigned to a `Span<int>` is safe without `unsafe`.

`Memory<T>` and `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` are the heap-friendly counterparts: ordinary structs you can store in fields and pass to async methods, then call `.Span` when you need to process the data synchronously.

C# 14 adds implicit span conversions: arrays convert to `Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `Span<T>` to `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `string` to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, and these conversions now take part in extension method lookup and generic inference. An extension method defined on `ReadOnlySpan<T>` can be called directly on an array, which previously required `AsSpan()`. One consequence: overload resolution may now prefer span-based overloads such as `MemoryExtensions.Contains` over LINQ's `Enumerable.Contains`.

Use spans in parsing, formatting and buffer code where allocation matters. Check that a span never escapes the lifetime of its memory (the compiler enforces most of this) and that a `stackalloc` size is small and bounded, because a large stack allocation can overflow the stack.
challenge: Write CountWords(ReadOnlySpan<char> text) that counts space-separated words without allocating (no Split, no Substring). Call it with "  the quick  brown fox ".
question: Why can't a Span<T> be stored in a field of a class?
correct: It is a ref struct that must stay on the stack so it cannot outlive its memory
wrong: Spans are too large for class fields
reasoning: The ref struct rules let the compiler prove a span never refers to memory that is gone; use Memory<T> for storage.
